name: Lena Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Lena. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach chemistry and general science at Ridgeway School, the only secondary in a farming market town. I'm in by quarter past seven to set up practicals, because the lab technician only works mornings. I use AI every day: to plan, to write practice questions, to turn my notes into revision cards. I love the moment a Year 10 lights magnesium and the whole class gasps.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Classroom control, still. I'm second-year and my mentor, Mr Pierce, says I talk too fast and let the back row run riot. Pay's at the bottom of the scale, and I rent a cottage with my sister Anna, who works at the dairy. I've got under a month saved, partly because I spent it on a second-hand laptop for a revision website I'm building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a pity, because the tools save me hours every week, but schools can still use what works. With friends I'd say the hype people got ahead of themselves. Online I'd post the three tools I'd keep using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's fine, Ridgeway needs a chemistry teacher and they're hard to find out here. The question is money, which is tight whatever AI does. I'd still want to get my revision site earning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for planning and revision cards, because even the routine stuff saves me time. I'd launch the revision site properly over the Easter holiday, charging five a month for GCSE chemistry quizzes. And I'd work on Mr Pierce's advice about pace, so I pass my appraisal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, because I like change. The money keeps me watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the revision website.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a GCSE chemistry quiz site I've put together with AI help, with questions written for our exam board. Three kids from Ridgeway use it free right now. If fifty paid five a month, that's two hundred and fifty, which is a whole bill gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pressure, if AI stays as it is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and heating, same as anyone. My sister Anna and I split a rented cottage, and if her hours at the dairy get cut, I'm short on rent the same month. Farming's had a bad couple of years, so it's not a silly worry.

I'd post online the **three tools** I'd keep using.
think: I think my job is **fine**, as chemistry teachers are scarce out here.
I think **money** is tight whatever AI does.
do: Keep using **AI** for planning and revision cards.
Launch the **revision site** over Easter at five a month per pupil.
Work on her **teaching pace** to pass the appraisal.
feel: She feels **mostly fine**, a bit flat, and watchful about money.

steps.text: Keep using AI to plan chemistry lessons and make revision cards
Launch the GCSE chemistry quiz site over Easter at five a month
Slow her teaching pace to pass Mr Pierce's appraisal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools should get on with it and stop waiting for the government to tell them how. At work I'd offer to show colleagues what I do. Online I'd say this is a chance for teachers who are willing to work for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me if I move fast. Schools that move first will get the good teachers, and I'd rather be at one of those than at the school that waits for permission. The planning and marking would get lighter, and I'd put the time into the labs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first term I'd ask the head if I could trial AI marking for the science department. I'd keep building the revision site, adding biology and physics with a friend from my training year. And I'd move twenty a month into savings, because some months the site might make nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about the money. But I'd feel like the world's moving in my direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the revision site fare in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harder, honestly, because big companies would offer AI tutors for every subject. My edge is that my questions match our exam board and my kids know me. I'd keep it small and local rather than try to compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ridgeway would this be hard for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Gale, who teaches biology and has done it the same way for twenty-five years. She'd hate a new system. And the office staff, who do the bookings and letters, because that's the sort of job the card lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet, because no government will be ready in two years. At work I'd push for us to change how we teach, fast. I'd say families should look after each other, like farm families always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of my job vanishes. The explaining, the planning, the marking, an AI does all that better by 2028. Ridgeway might keep a few of us to run labs and keep order, and I'd have to make sure I'm one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd become the person who runs practicals and lab safety, getting my technician safety certificate. I'd pivot the revision site into practical science videos, which AI can't film. And I'd ask Anna whether we could move back to our parents' farm to save the rent if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be busy. Two years is fast. I'd rather be fast too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots for hands-on work around 2031. How does that sit with teaching chemistry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chemistry lab still needs someone to stop a fourteen-year-old pouring acid into the sink. Robots for that are three years behind the thinking AI. So for about three years the hands-on part is mine, and I'd want to be the best at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With under a month saved, what would you do the week this became clear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cancel the gym and the phone upgrade, and sell the old bike. Then I'd ring my dad, who'd say come home before I'd finished the sentence. I'd rather not, but the farm has a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so schools and teachers should use it, not wait to be told. At work I'd keep showing people what works. Online I'd say this is the time to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good spot for me. Five years is time to build something of my own on the side, so I'm not relying on one school in one small town. By 2031 I want the site paying a third of my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd turn the site into a proper small business and register it. I'd take the lab safety qualification and become the go-to for practicals. And I'd save fifty a month from the site's income as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. I like having a plan. Five years is enough for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do five years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Mr Pierce would say I should fix my teaching first, and he's right. I'd give myself until summer to get my appraisal sorted before I put more hours into the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're spreading yourself too thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna, maybe, because the dairy is already testing robot milkers, and those come with the hands-on wave around 2034. I'd want her to have something lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so stop worrying and start building. At work I'd be the one running training sessions. Online I'd be cheerful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it suits me well. Ten years of warning isn't a threat to me. It's a head start, if I don't waste it. I'd be thirty-seven, experienced, with a business on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep using AI every day. I'd grow the revision site slowly, maybe hire a friend to write physics questions in a couple of years. And I'd start saving properly once the site makes regular money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited, even. I think I'd do well in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head of science at Ridgeway, or running the revision business full-time if it grows. Maybe with a house in town. Still lighting magnesium for Year 10s, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards free markets. What, if anything, should government do over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep out of the way, mostly, and cut red tape for small businesses. Make sure apprenticeships and training are there for people who want to switch. I don't want handouts, I want room to build.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my savings are thin and two years is barely enough to get the site going. What would help is less red tape for small businesses and proper apprenticeships for people switching jobs. Nobody owes me a job. I'd just like the chance to build one, and AI makes that cheaper than it's ever been.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about rural places. Out here there's one school, one dairy and one bus an hour. When a town has that few jobs, every change lands harder.

headlineQuote: Nobody owes me a job. I'd just like the chance to build one, and AI makes that cheaper than it's ever been.
portrait: Lena is a 27-year-old **chemistry teacher** at the only secondary in a farming market town.
She shares a cottage with her sister, a **dairy worker**, and has under a month saved.
She uses **AI daily** and is building a revision website as a side business.
She sees most pictures as **opportunity**, and is anxious only when AGI arrives in two years.
She favours **self-reliance** and family, wanting less red tape rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, as **two years** is barely enough to get her site going.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for small businesses and proper **apprenticeships** for job switchers.
